#5791. America’s New Shipbuilding Orders Are Expensive Bets on Fossil Freight

South Korea’s Hanwha Group owns the Philadelphia shipyard that has become a centerpiece of Washington’s attempt to rebuild American commercial shipbuilding. Its Hanwha Ocean and Hanwha Systems subsidiaries acquired the US yard in December 2024. The investment creates and sustains American production capacity and jobs while transferring shipbuilding expertise, technology and training from South Korea to US workers. The facility is in America, but its corporate ownership remains South Korean. The company’s published orderbook, however, tells a more complicated story: two liquefied natural gas carriers, four firm orders for oil and chemical tankers, and options for another six tankers. Three LNG-fueled container ships ordered by Matson in 2022 predate the current administration. The newer LNG and tanker orders come from Hanwha’s own shipping affiliates. They can help restart production, but buying ships from another company in the same group does not demonstrate that independent shipowners will pay US construction prices.

The price gap is difficult to dismiss. Kinder Morgan’s January 2026 investor presentation estimates that a new medium-range Jones Act tanker would cost more than $240 million and require a long-term charter above $115,000 per day to justify construction. The existing charter market was around $90,000 per day. Kinder Morgan operates 16 tankers, with its fleet fully utilized, yet the gap between current charter revenue and the cost of a replacement vessel remains substantial. High utilization establishes a need for shipping services; it does not establish a financeable order for a new American-built tanker at today’s prices.

Coastal petroleum shipping also competes with other domestic infrastructure. A 2025 report to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission estimated moving gasoline from Houston to New York Harbor at under 8 cents per gallon by pipeline, about 20 cents by ship, and roughly 35 cents by rail. These illustrative route costs do not cover every destination, and tankers remain essential where pipelines are unavailable. They do show why expensive new tankers cannot count on charter customers accepting whatever price domestic construction requires. Longer term, the International Energy Agency estimates that electric vehicles displaced 1.7 million barrels of oil per day worldwide in 2025 and could displace about 5 million by 2030 under its policy scenarios. That does not mean US tanker demand vanishes, but fleet investment must account for changes in the cargo market over several decades.

LNG export carriers have a more plausible near-term growth market, although their prospects are different from the prospects of LNG-fueled container ships. US gas exports may expand, and LNG tankers will be needed to carry them. The commercial test for a US-built LNG carrier is whether it can win an arm’s-length contract against established Korean, Japanese and Chinese shipyards. Hanwha’s plan to train Philadelphia workers through its Korean shipyards can strengthen US industrial capability, and affiliated orders can provide an initial production run. The central uncertainty is whether independent buyers will still choose these ships once the group’s internal demand and any cargo preference are removed.

A broader domestic vessel market already exists. US-flag Great Lakes freighters carried 71.3 million tons in 2025, much of it iron ore, limestone, cement, coal and other bulk materials. Those cargo flows will change as steelmaking and energy systems evolve, while ferry services, harbour vessels, inland cargo craft and multipurpose ships will still require renewal. Battery-electric and hybrid-electric propulsion offer practical options on routes with manageable energy requirements and reliable charging access. Large, long-distance bulk ships need a more selective technology assessment, rather than an assumption that every vessel can run on batteries.

Recent projects demonstrate what a committed customer can contribute to ship economics. CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept launched an electric inland barge in Vietnam for a 180-kilometre round trip. Nike agreed to fill 90% of its capacity for eight years, helping justify a vessel reportedly costing about twice as much as its diesel equivalent. A dedicated charging installation and renewable electricity form part of the service. That is a commercially structured freight proposition, with its higher capital cost supported by contracted utilization and expected operating savings.

Electric propulsion does not cure the American shipbuilding cost problem by itself. Washington State’s three new hybrid-electric ferries carry a $714.5 million shipbuilding contract, and the state’s estimate including additional equipment and other program expenses is approximately $1.15 billion. Construction has started; the ferries are not yet in service. The path to a productive shipbuilding industry still runs through standardized designs, modular fabrication, trained workers, repeat orders, reliable delivery and falling labor-hours per vessel. It would be a mistake to treat electrification as a substitute for manufacturing reform.

Hanwha’s South Korean capital and know-how could contribute to that reform by developing US suppliers and production skills that serve several vessel classes. That is a meaningful way to rebuild domestic capability even though the parent company remains foreign-owned. Its progress should ultimately be measured by independent repeat customers, improving construction costs and commercially competitive vessels, rather than affiliated orders or investment announcements. A US maritime strategy anchored to the fossil-fuel cargoes of today risks missing a growing opportunity to build modern domestic vessels for the freight, port and ferry services of tomorrow.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Hanwha’s orders, Kinder Morgan’s tanker economics and the market for repeatable electric and hybrid maritime construction. It follows my earlier analysis of the Jones Act’s shipbuilding capacity gap.

#5790. The Buick Engine That Helped Launch The SR-71 Blackbird

The Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird spy plane is capable of flying 2,193.2 mph with a ceiling above 85,000 feet. To achieve those feats, it packed a pair of Pratt & Whitney J58 turbojets to enjoy a combined 50,000 pounds of thrust, and it even used a new kind of fuel that could withstand the friction from those blistering speeds. However, getting those mighty motors to turn over in the first place was no simple task, which is where the Buick Nailhead comes into play. It might not have directly powered the plane, but its earliest flights were only possible thanks to the engine.

A turbine engine requires a certain amount of airflow to ensure the fuel first ignites properly, and it has to reach a certain speed before the combustion process can sustain itself. As a result, the turbojet engines need to begin spinning even before they're operating on their own. But these are massive mills weighing in at 6,000 pounds each, so a simple electric starter like the one in a traditional car wouldn't have the strength to get the job done. A pair of Buick engines, on the other hand, would be enough to give its turbines the power they needed.

The mill used to get the Blackbird's own engines spinning was a 401-cubic-inch Nailhead, which can pound out 325 horses and 445 pound-feet of torque. The Air Force used a pair of those motors on the Blackbird's original start cart, yoking them together with a 12-inch-wide belt joining their transmissions. The combined output was then fed to the jets via mechanical linkage, spinning them up to their proper running speed. The pilot would then ignite the engines, allowing the Blackbird to run on its own from there.

We've previously explained how the Buick Nailhead V8 got its name; the tops of its vertically oriented valves looked like, well, nailheads. The first-gen motor from 1953 had a displacement of 322 cubic inches, and an example with 264 cubic inches came to be when the brand introduced the Buick Special the next year. That latter setup had a pretty short life, as it was out of production after 1955. The Nailheads then began their climb up the displacement ladder. From 1957 to 1961, Buick raised the bar to 364 cubic inches. There was also a 425-cubic-inch Nailhead V8 on the roster from 1963 to 1966, backed by 360 horsepower with its optional dual-quad carburetor setup.

The 401, though, was especially popular. Among the first cars with this engine under their hoods were the 1959 Buick Invicta and Electra. It's also worth noting that, in the Invicta, the motor gained the Wildcat 445 nickname for its impressive torque rating. The Invicta Wildcat that premiered in 1962 (and became the Buick Wildcat in 1963) relied on that mill to help boost the brand's performance credibility.

The striking first-generation Buick Riviera would boast the 401 Nailhead in 1963, as would the Skylark Gran Sport when it arrived in 1965. The Skylark GS represents the point where Buick went all-in on the 401's performance potential — at least from a marketing standpoint. Even though its engine's output was unchanged from previous Buicks, the Skylark GS is considered to be Buick's first muscle car. Production of the engine itself would meet its end by the next year, but its use in the Blackbird would continue for a much longer period of time.

The Buick Nailhead engines would go on to power plenty of dragsters, too, building a proven track record for delivering low-end torque. Remember, that Wildcat 445 exceeded a pound-foot of twist for every cubic inch of displacement. When you also consider the Nailhead's reputation for long-term reliability, it's no surprise that it worked so well on Blackbird duty.

Yet, after roughly a decade on the start cart, the Nailheads would be retired in the 1970s and replaced by two other power-packed GM V8 engines. These were 454-cubic-inch big-block LS7 V8s that had originally been engineered to bring 460 horses to the 1970 Chevrolet Corvette. A combination of circumstances kept that motor out of regular production entirely, but that didn't prevent the Air Force from snagging a pair. (As a side note, those LS7 big-blocks were unrelated to the more recent LS7 Corvette engine that defied small-block limits in the C6 Z06.)

Finally, in the 1980s, the Air Force would move to a technology that had been around since about three decades prior: the pneumatic starter. Rather than bringing the turbine up to operating speed with a direct mechanical connection, these work by forcing high-pressure air through the turbine blades — like blowing a stream of air across a pinwheel. The Blackbird relied on pneumatic starters from then on, until its retirement the 1990s.

#5789. As Jackery Inventory Sells Out, Are Portable Batteries Set To Take Off?

I recently wrote reviews of the new Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2 and Explorer 100D. A few days later, a connection with Jackery messaged me that their Black Friday/Cyber Monday products had largely sold out. Just three days after launching on November 1. This includes 1000, 2000, 3600 and 5000 portable power and solar generator models. Additional models have sold out since then or will likely sell out soon. The recently launched Explorer 100D is still available in limited quantities at Walmart and Costco.

While Jackery will still take orders for Black Friday/Cyber Monday sales, most models currently listed for purchase will be on a preorder basis. Customers should check estimated delivery dates. Some restocking is expected in late November, although broader inventory availability may not recover until early next year.

While much of America was recovering from Halloween and election victory parties, portable batteries were selling out. This wasn’t the result of limited supply, but rather a massive, unanticipated increase in demand.

Between October 19th  and 26th, Jackery retail sales increased 755% at Costco, 106% at Walmart, 297% at The Home Depot and 442% at Lowes. For added perspective, at Costco alone, sales increased from 2379 to 20,343 over that one week.

Jackery is looking into what’s behind the massive increase in demand. Clearly, there have been climate-related disasters over the past year, including hurricanes and wildfires. Jackery’s collaboration with the Red Cross helps illustrate the benefits of portable power in emergency response. However, that only partially explains the growth. A related potential explanation is the growing push for household preparedness.  There are reports of at least 17 countries encouraging people to keep three to seven days of food, water and other essentials. Winter storm season, grid strain and rising energy costs could be stoking fears of potential power outages. The US FORTRESS America initiative has also added an emphasis on resilience. Together, these signals may be pushing “preparedness” beyond food and water to include power.

Preparedness is gaining emphasis with power becoming an increasingly important part of being prepared. The fear of “what if” can be a powerful motivator. Having backup power can keep the air handlers working for people’s furnaces. People on well water can keep the pumps running. Backup power can keep refrigerators full of food from spoiling.

Overall, Jackery is the global leader in solar generator sales volume and was named the “World’s No.1 Solar Generator Brand” by Frost & Sullivan. With over 15 years of experience and extensive safety protocols, the brand is well established. For the purchase of a product that manages risks, having a trusted brand is clearly valuable.

Although there has not been a detailed study of the consumer motivations, preparedness is likely a major motivator. However, versatile portable power stations have additional benefits. I keep finding new ways to use the HomePower 1000 Plus V2. And new possible benefits keep opening up.

Beyond providing emergency power, I can take power with me. I can set up an office remotely. I can run and recharge tools away from an outlet. I can power a radiant heater for a few hours while sitting outdoors. I can power an air conditioner for hours or run a fan all day. I can make coffee and cook food. In many ways, the batteries can replace functions once covered not just by a generator, but also a campfire or grill.

While using the battery, I also became more aware of my electricity usage. Seeing how quickly different appliances deplete the battery makes me realize where my utility bill is really going. Some things use less electricity than I anticipated, and some use far more. That awareness helps me to reduce my overall consumption.

And the UPS function can also save delicate equipment, as well as any work on computers and other machinery during a power disruption. I personally would not run a large print on my 3D printer without the backup battery. Providing stable power can extend the lifespan of many expensive devices.

The ability to integrate solar panels provides an additional level of preparedness, allowing the battery to be recharged by the sun when grid power is not available. However, solar can also charge the battery for daily use. While this may not yet be able to feed into the grid without additional equipment, people can reasonably use solar power fed into the battery to replace grid power at the point of use. When the regulations are figured out, balcony solar could expand the possibilities. All this can reduce people’s energy costs.

The battery can provide power when they need it, rather than just when the sun is shining. And when connected to the grid with a time of use (TOU) plan, it can charge when electricity is inexpensive and provide power when it is expensive. The savings from this alone could pay for the battery and start saving people money on their utility bills. And the grid becomes more stable in the process.

If the current battery capacity is not enough, Jackery makes expandible batteries to add more capacity.

In addition, the portable, scalable batteries can form the foundation of a whole home system. With greater utility communication, the added capacity could open up new possibilities for users to benefit while they help stabilize the grid. And they still benefit from the backup power. In addition, after seeing the capabilities, some people may even be inspired to look into going off-grid.

Of course, Jackery is likely not the only company seeing a surge in sales. I hope consumer demand and adoption is rising across the board. With a low barrier to entry and the ability to provide a level of preparedness, sales of portable batteries are likely to continue to grow.

Jackery is actively focused on removing the barriers to entry. Then the benefits of battery backup and portable power can be realized by more people. As more people see the benefits of portable expandable batteries, more people will want them. As more battery capacity is deployed, more applications can become viable. That not only has the ability to make homes more resilient, but also to build a more resilient grid. With the ability to shift consumption through distributed storage, more renewable energy can be utilized.

People who may have bought originally for preparedness will start to realize the broader benefits of their purchase. When people benefit from something, they will tend to rationalize it. This typically works better to change perspectives than trying to start with a rational argument. When people feel the relief of having backup power available for “what if,” they can then expand upon that with greater feelings of independence. Once they personally benefit from the storage that enables greater renewable adoption, they may increase their support for renewable energy. By addressing fears of “what if,” people may open themselves to thinking about “what’s possible.”

Of course, this might just be a temporary sales blip. But it could also be the start of a rapid expansion in home battery use. That could open up a wide range of new possibilities.

#5787. Conventional Vs. Transit Design: Why Some School Buses Have Flat Fronts

School buses haven't changed much since 1939, but they came a long way before then. Some of the first vehicles used to take kids to school were simply horse-drawn wagons. It wasn't until the start of World War I that the first motorized buses seem to have appeared in this country. That's when a company called Wayne Works introduced a model in 1914. It was built on a long-wheelbase Model T chassis, so its engine was in the traditional location, under the hood up front.

Fast-forward a few years and we find Crown Coach evolving the concept of motorized school buses even further. Crown was a major commercial-vehicle manufacturer, founded in 1903 to sell business wagons to businessmen. It would survive all the way up to 1990 by building not only buses, but also hearses, fire trucks, bakery trucks, ambulances, and even airplanes.

Crown brought some notable innovations to the bus field as well. For example, it introduced the forward-control school bus in 1932. This wasn't the first forward-control bus of any type in the country, though. A firm called Twin Coach has that honor. The company had already been building flat-faced delivery trucks, and during the Depression, it brought the layout to its small buses — including some meant for municipal transit.

The head start for flat-faced city buses meant that when flat-faced school buses became popular, folks looked back to the first application to name the second. The new wave of so-called transit-style school buses gave school districts a new way to transport kids, with both new advantages and new drawbacks compared to conventional school buses.

First off, let's deal with their industry classifications: Class C buses are conventional buses, with engines in front and the main exit/entrance located behind the front wheels. The flat-front buses are in Class D and can theoretically have their engines anywhere from beside the driver to the very back of the bus. In the real world, positioning the motor at the rear is a big-time benefit to driver and students alike. That way, they face less noise, heat, and air pollution.

The transit-style layout also improves the driver's vision, since there's no massive hood to see over and around. Conventional buses are more like those big pickups with huge frontal blind spots that just keep getting larger as the years go by. Additionally, the flat-face setup maximizes how many passengers can fit in a given footprint. The difference isn't huge, but the flat-face buses can generally fit up to 90 passengers while conventional versions max out at about 77 to 83.

For their part, the traditional buses tend to be more maneuverable than their alternatives. This is partly due to their different wheelbases and how they can change a vehicle's handling. Looking at data from the Bureau of Transportation, Class C conventional buses with a recommended wheelbase of about 21.3 feet have noticeably shorter turning radii than Class D transit-style models, with recommended wheelbases of 23 feet. Lower maintenance costs are another strong suit of the conventional buses, as it's much easier to access their engines.

In the end, the reason you'll see conventional buses in some places and transit-style versions elsewhere is a matter of local preference. But neither class is likely to save kids from traumatic school bus stories.

#5785. Saving The Manuals: Porsche's Mechanical MECOSA Vs. Ferrari's Electronic Manuale Tech

Sometimes even an exotic carmaker's answer to a challenge might say something about future cars for the proletariat. Most of us probably can't even afford a replacement shift knob on the 2027 $677,600 Ferrari 12Cilindri Manuale, but how Ferrari and Porsche are adapting their automatics to fit manual transmissions could one day portend stick-shifts for us all. Here's the reason to even posit this: Carmakers want a cheaper way to build hybrids, EVs, and gas cars on the same platform and on the same assembly line. Adding or subtracting parts will make that too costly — which may result in them just ditching any manual effort, if that's the only solution.

Now that you understand the why of this reporting, we'll also acknowledge why some readers are freaking out about the fact that the 12Cilindri Manuale will simulate the experience of shifting. It's not a conventional manual, and we'll explain how it works in greater depth, but the gist is that Ferrari's linking an electric stalk and faux clutch pedal to an eight-speed dual-clutch drivetrain. It's as real (or fake) as paddle shifters, just via a dongle and pedal.

On the other hand, Porsche's stick-shift retrofit is a hack of their seven-speed PDK, which stands for Porsche dual clutch– or Doppelkupplung. It debuted on the 2020 Porsche 911 Carrera S Manual, dubbed MECOSA, which is Porsche-speak for MEchanically COnverted Shift Actuator, and is an entirely mechanical retrofit, featuring a seven-speed gated shifter and third pedal. But which is better? And which foreshadows a future joystick for the masses?

Automatics have been steadily growing in popularity since their debut in 1939, and according to the U.S. Department of Energy, by 2022, 99% of all new cars sold offered automatics. Standard automatics further evolved in 1987, with the introduction of the gearless CVT — a transmission Jalopnik readers hate in a way that borders on irrational.

The alternative? Something like Porsche's PDK, which is a dual-clutch manu-matic. Porsche began experimenting with the PDK in the 1980s. It debuted in racing in the 1986 962, and by 2008 you could get a PDK in a 911, which allowed drivers to shift using paddles for extra engagement and provided benefits such as engine braking. But it does more than just ditch the third pedal and shifter — the PDK in the 2020 Carrera S shifts at least 200% faster than a human can shift in the MECOSA, according to Car and Driver.

Despite that, at least 20% of Porsche 911 customers in America opt for a genuine manual, hence the MECOSA. Mind you, this is still a PDK underneath, and since its gears are arranged for a computer to actuate, not a human, they're not in any sane order. Instead, the pattern looks like this, starting from the top left of the gate: R,2,3,1,6,4,5,7. To translate the driver's inputs into proper shifts behind the scenes, MECOSA activates a jangle of cables and shafts so that each push or pull of the shifter engages the correct gear.

It's a solution that would make MacGyver proud. It is also not one Porsche is sticking with. The Stuttgart giant isn't abandoning its 911 customers clamoring for a manual; but now, you can get a Carrera S with a standard six-speed transmission, rather than a seven-speed with a Rube Goldberg machine tacked on.

Like Porsche, Ferrari's Manuale has a gated shifter instead of paddles, and it gains a third pedal on the floor. The transmission is physically identical to that of the paddle-shift version. Ferrari's legerdemain is to delete the paddles, insert a shift knob, and add a clutch pedal with sprung feedback. Now it feels as if your left foot is encountering a clutch spring as your ankle hinges, and Ferrari has created similar tricks in the gated shifter itself to simulate the feeling of gear shifts. Behind the scenes, however, sensors track both inputs. Your motions tell the car's computers what to do, which is identical to what happens when you pilot the 12Cilindri minus the Manuale. Except, in this one, it's possible to encounter rough shifts and even to stall the Manuale.

Keep in mind, this V12 Ferrari is carrying two extra gears you cannot joystick into. This is still actually an eight-speed DCT, not a six-speed manual, so it can also be driven like an automatic. Tap the D button on the console and the car will shift itself, and you have access to seventh and eighth gear — for lower-rpm Autobahn sprints, say.

You might cry in your pasta fagioli that Ferrari should only sell its 819-horsepower, 9,250-rpm V12 with a genuine-article manual gearbox, but Ferrari will only make 1,499 units of the Manuale. For that take rate, there was no way they were going to retrofit a manual gearbox, if for no other reason than this: It probably saves them millions on not having to develop a separate manual transmission 12Cilindri or certify two different transmissions for regulators.

Right now, the electric Porsche Taycan gets an E-Shift option. The Hyundai Ioniq 5 N offers something similar. E-Shift uses software to simulate gear changes, including simulating step-changes in acceleration, and adding a soundtrack, just like the Hyundai. Porsche copied patterns from their PDK, including adding a deceleration function during downshifts. But neither brand adds a third pedal — yet.

But the future for Porsche probably isn't either E-Shift or conventional manuals, since Porsche recently published two patents that seem to follow in Ferrari's footsteps, creating simulated shifting that could function in electric, hybrid, and gas cars. The patents also mention a fake clutch pedal, just like the one Ferrari is using, and the ability to shift sequentially, like the PDK. Porsche also describes a system that uses electrical components to provide resistance and something like progressive feel to gear swaps, to enliven driver engagement.

Considering what we found in our review of the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, with its fake shifts and sounds, it only makes sense that blurring slushbox convenience and manual control at the flip of a switch could make any machine more entertaining — or more relaxing. Porsche's patents could also potentially smoke Ferrari's hack, because they apply regardless of powertrain.

This innovation could also get to non-Porsche EVs and hybrids via licensing. After all, Porsche isn't doing great financially. Ditto, parent company, Volkswagen — partly thanks to Porsche's struggles. A little trademark cash could definitely help that picture. And, just maybe, save the manuals for the rest of us.

#5784. Alas, Poor Cybertruck, We Hardly Knew Thee

If you felt a ripple in the space-time continuum yesterday, yes, the rumors are true. All too sadly true. The Tesla Cybertruck, introduced to motorists in 2019 with great fanfare and a sales goal of up to 250,000 units per year, is slated to cross the rainbow bridge into the dustbine of automotive history sometime next year. Not to worry, Tesla fans, rumor has it that Tesla’s Cybercab robotaxi will pick up where the Cybertruck left off — oh, wait. Hold, please…

Tesla is notoriously shy about releasing sales figures, but there are ways to reach an approximation. Earlier this year CleanTechnica calculated that the Cybertruck barely scraped by 2025 with just 17,012 units delivered. Even so, just one year earlier Tesla CEO Elon Musk was still pitching the 250,000 Cybertrucks-per-year goal.

Even though it is soon to be gone, the Cybertruck will never be forgotten. Much in the same way as the Edsel, “Cybertruck” will linger on as shorthand for a fabulously hyped product without an audience.

The Cybertruck was promised as a full sized, five-seat electric pickup truck with ample storage room. Tesla delivered on the zero emission angle, of course, and the five seats, too. However, the automaker failed to deliver on pickup truckyness in any substantive way (see entire CleanTechnica archive here).

So … don’t let the door hit you on the way out. Multiple electric pickup trucks are taking up the space left by the Cybertruck, including the forthcoming Ford Fathom alongside offerings from Rivian, Slate Auto, and other automakers.

Elon Musk himself announced the untimely death of the Cybertruck in a post on his social media site X earlier today.

“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk stated somewhat blandly, perhaps expecting his audience to appreciate the good news about “increased Cybercab production.”

If so, Musk was probably disappointed to hear from X users like Ben McCombe, who skipped over the implication that the Cybercap would occupy more space in the Tesla Gigafactory in Austin, Texas. Instead, he zeroed in on the Cybertruck in a particularly pithy comment:

“Installed tooling to build 125k Cybertrucks a year.

“Made just $100m in gross profits from sales.

Tesla’s stock tanked on November 3 and the following two days, after Democratic candidates dominated the all-important mid-term elections in both Houses of Congress, and in statehouses across the country, including Tesla’s home state, Texas. The power shift all but guarantees a more vigorous application of federal and state regulations governing Tesla’s products and operations.

Still, the automaker scored a partial recovery just a few days later. Tesla stock was swinging upwards as of midday on November 6, with Musk’s Cybercab announcement possibly factored into the partial recovery. However, those incoming lawmakers are going to be taking a close look at the Cybercab, and so far the picture is not pretty.

One sign of trouble emerged on September 3, when Musk failed to appear at a long-anticipated Cybercab launch event in Texas. The very next day, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration went out of its way to let everyone know that it is investigating Tesla’s self-certification for the Cybercab under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act.

“The US Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) today announced that it has opened an Audit Query (AQ) to investigate Tesla’s certification that its new Cybercab meets all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS),” NHTSA announced on September 4.

NHTSA initially gave Tesla until September 30 to respond to a list of 21 questions about the Cybercab self-certification, then extended the deadline to October 30.

Anyone eager to learn how automakers go about self-certifying new models under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act will be sorely disappointed, unless they are privileged to read the documents Tesla finally submitted. “The tricky part is that in its public response, Tesla offered one whole sentence. ‘The entirety of this file is confidential business information,'” Carscoops reported earlier today.

So close and yet so far. While the Cybercab investigation is still bubbling away on the backburner, Tesla has also set itself up for a whole ‘nother round of investigations related to its newly unveiled “flying car,” part of a suite of high-end sports cars modeled after the original Tesla Roadster.

The Roadster reboot was slightly clouded by the release of a new documentary on Elon Musk’s rise to both automotive and political power, but just slightly. The automotive press went nuts over the spectacle of the new Tesla Roadster rocket going airborne for a few seconds, then safely landing on all four tires with an assist from SpaceX-designed thrusters.

Whether or not that actually counts as a flight or just a thruster-enhanced jump, the Federal Aviation Administration has already stated that the rocket does not meet its definition of an aircraft.

As of for the question of whether or not the vehicle can be used on public roads, that’s something for the NTHSA to weigh in on. On Tesla’s part, though, the automaker has reportedly stated that the rocket is not designed for use on public roads. That seems to cut NTHSA out of the picture, though some industry observers have suggested that the agency could adopt a framework that encompasses vehicles with thrusters.

Musk himself has suggested that anyone who purchases the thruster-equipped Roadster can make it fly on a purpose-built tack on Tesla (or perhaps SpaceX) property, presumably in Texas.

The land use issue opens up a whole ‘nother can of worms regarding Musk’s operations in Texas. If anything, the offer of an off-road rocket track seems to let Tesla off the hook for the actions of any rambunctious rocket driver who insists on trialing the car on public roads.

For the record, Musk the movie opened initially in Los Angeles and New York City on October 9. A wide release on hundreds of screens was scheduled for October 16, but the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, abruptly pulled back on the plan under new ownership. On October 27, representatives for the film contacted CleanTechnica to clarify that the Musk documentary was still showing on scores of screens around the country even after the dial-down. Either way, if you missed it in theaters, you can catch the whole thing — including the Cybertruck debacle and so much more — streaming as of today, November 6, on Amazon Prime Video, iTunes, and YouTube along with cable services.

#5782. You Officially Missed Your Chance To Buy A New Toyota Supra Or BMW Z4

We all knew this day was coming, but none of us wanted to face it; the MkV Toyota Supra and G29 BMW Z4 are officially off the new car market. Our friends at CarsDirect analyzed national dealer inventory data on Tuesday and found that there are no more new Supras or Z4s on dealer lots across the United States. Both models were built at the Magna Steyr contract manufacturing facility in Austria, but their production run concluded in spring of this year. At least both manufacturers commemorated the end of production with Final Editions, but we're still sad to see both nameplates join the great new car lot in the sky. For now, at least.

Toyota Motor North America's senior vice president of product planning and strategy Cooper Ericksen told MotorTrend that a Supra successor is coming, but that there will be another hiatus in the iconic sports car's legacy. Ericksen said, "it is our goal to have a gap that is significantly less [than the last one]." That last gap between the fourth-generation Supra and the fifth-generation car lasted an excruciating 20 years, so hopefully the sixth-generation Supra comes much sooner than that. Sadly BMW has not publicly announced plans for a fourth-generation Z4 as of now.

The fourth-generation of BMW's Z4 hit the streets of a very different world eight years ago in 2019, and offered the classic long-nose, short-deck sports car design solely in ragtop form. The GR Supra debuted a year later in 2020, and caused quite a buzz among car enthusiasts for its Bavarian lineage, but quickly proved it was still true to the Supra formula as a powerful two-seat driver's car. BMW sold just 2,113 Z4s in 2025, and Toyota managed to shift slightly more Supras at 2,953, but neither figure is particularly impressive or cost effective, especially considering that pricey platform updates would be necessary to conform to changing regulations.

The automotive industry has been a bit unsteady as of late, affecting even industry stalwarts like BMW and Toyota. BMW slashed its outlook for 2026 in June, and typical sales leader Toyota just posted its third-straight month of sales declines despite simultaneously raising its annual earnings forecast.

Fortunately BMW isn't leaving driving enthusiasts out to dry, with the launch of its Neue Klasse vehicles including the highly anticipated iX3 electric crossover and a new iteration of the always titillating 3 Series sedan. Toyota isn't abandoning driving enthusiasts either, with a new Celica in the works. In the meantime, BMW has an array of performance cars including the excellent M2, M3, and M4, and Toyota has the hilariously fun GR Corolla and GR86, but we'll still miss the Z4 and Supra.

TAMPA, Fla. — On Thursday, November 5, Sierra Club Florida and partner organizations hosted “Power & Perspectives: The Energy Dialogue,” a community town hall addressing TECO bill increases and the need for local utility accountability. Over 25 people attended the event featuring a panel of Sierra Club, Food & Water Watch, and Hillsborough Affordable Energy Coalition representatives, as well as a member of Tampa’s City Council and the city’s Sustainability & Resilience Officer.

TECO has recently boasted rate decreases, however, monthly bills for residential or small business customers using 1,000 kWh per month are still over $10 higher than in December 2024. While families contend with higher bills, the CEO of TECO made $2.5 million last year. The CEO of Emera, TECO’s parent company, made $9.5 million.

“Transparency shouldn’t be optional when families are forced to choose between keeping the lights on and buying groceries,” said Walter Smith II, Sierra Club’s Tampa Bay Organizing Representative. “We invited our neighbors, TECO reps, and environmental justice experts into the same room because the community deserves answers about their energy burdens and the various impacts of fossil fuels on our environment and health. This town hall is a critical first step toward demanding a just, affordable, and clean energy future for everyone in Tampa Bay.”

“Tampa residents have been struggling under the weight of skyrocketing electricity bills, all while Tampa Electric walks away with record profits year after year and passes the costs of fuel, storm recovery, and even its brand new Midtown headquarters onto ratepayers,” said Isabella Moeller, Florida Organizer for Food & Water. “But our community has had enough. TECO is a for-profit company beholden to shareholders only, that’s why we’re making a wide call to our local elected officials to hold TECO and its regulators accountable to the people they serve. Tampa City Council has an opportunity to pass an affordable energy resolution that commits the city to opposing TECO’s unjust rate hikes and supporting clean, affordable energy solutions. We must build on this momentum and ensure that affordable energy is a priority for every elected official in Tampa.”

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person's right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. #5780. Lumateperone Brings Rapid Relief in Bipolar Mania

— The atypical antipsychotic improved symptoms within 3 days

Lumateperone (Caplyta) rapidly improved symptoms of acute mania associated with bipolar I disorder, a phase III trial showed.

Among 351 patients with or without mixed features, lumateperone demonstrated superiority over placebo in reducing the Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) total score by day 22 (least squares mean difference -3.7, 95% CI -5.61 to -1.86, P<0.0001), with significant differences noted by day 3 and maintained from week 1 onward, reported Roger S. McIntyre, MD, of the University of Toronto, and colleagues.

Meeting the key secondary endpoint, the atypical antipsychotic also led to greater improvement in overall illness severity, demonstrating superiority over placebo in change in Clinical Global Impression-Severity (CGI-S) score (least squares mean difference -0.4, 95% CI -0.58 to -0.17, P=0.0003).

The study was presented at the Neuroscience Education Institute (NEI) Fall Congress in Colorado Springs, Colorado.

"The overall clinical meaningfulness was not only observed rapidly on day 3, which was the second day post-treatment, but also response rates that translate into a number needed to treat of 5, indicating clinical relevance," McIntyre told MedPage Today.

"These efficacy findings alongside low rates of treatment-emergent adverse events and discontinuation rates due to adverse events, similar to placebo, underscore the clinical utility of lumateperone and why it would be a preferred treatment in adults presenting with mania with or without mixed features," he said.

This was the second pivotal phase III study evaluating lumateperone for acute bipolar mania. Its findings replicate and reinforce results from an identically designed sister trial reported in September at Psych Congress.

The once-daily, oral antipsychotic is not currently approved for the treatment of manic episodes associated with bipolar I disorder, but is approved for adults with bipolar depression (as monotherapy or adjunctive therapy with lithium or valproate), for schizophrenia, and as an adjunctive therapy with antidepressants for major depressive disorder.

While the mechanism of action of lumateperone is unknown, its efficacy could be mediated through a combination of antagonist activity at central serotonin 5-HT2A receptors and partial agonist activity at central dopamine D2 receptors.

"With respect to existing knowledge of lumateperone, these data establish the efficacy of lumateperone across the mood spectrum," said McIntyre.

"Notwithstanding options available for the treatment of bipolar mania with and without mixed features in adults, there remains a need for treatments that are rapidly efficacious with meaningful improvements for what effectively is a medical emergency, that is, bipolar mania," he noted.

Michael Thase, MD, of the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, previously underscored in a statement from the drugmaker that "mania is among the most dangerous and worrisome phases of bipolar disorder, and treating it effectively takes more than partial or temporary relief of symptoms; it means bringing the episode itself under control as quickly as possible."

For the double-blind trial, eligible patients diagnosed with bipolar I disorder and an acute manic episode with or without mixed features (symptoms of mania or hypomania along with symptoms of depression) according to DSM-5-TR criteria were randomized 1:1 to receive 3 weeks of either lumateperone 42 mg or placebo. Treatment began in an inpatient setting, with patients eligible for discharge to outpatient care after week 2.

Average patient age was 46.1 years, and 56.1% were men. About 44% experienced five or more lifetime manic episodes, and a third were diagnosed with mixed features. Both groups had severe mania at baseline according to mean YMRS scores.

Nearly twice as many participants in the lumateperone group achieved treatment response, defined as a 50% or greater reduction in YMRS score (43.9% vs 23.7%, P<0.0001). More patients on treatment also met qualifications for remission, defined as a YMRS score of 12 or less (25.4% vs 16.4%, P=0.0330).

"The efficacy, tolerability, and safety record accords with what we have seen previously in bipolar depression and schizophrenia," said McIntyre.

The most common treatment-emergent adverse events with lumateperone versus placebo were dizziness (10.4% vs 1.7%), dry mouth (5.8% vs 1.1%), and somnolence (5.2% vs 1.7%). Discontinuation rates due to adverse events were low (4.0% vs 3.4%).

#5779. 5 Of The Biggest Gas Discounts Available Through Reward Programs Right Now

Since Trump's war with Iran kicked off in February of this year, gas prices have been on everyone's mind. Who could've predicted we'd see gas prices skyrocket as the result of such a war? Well, we did. Worry not, though, dear reader. Gas prices are sure to come crashing down any moment, especially now that three tankers have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Maybe after such a flawless victory, we should start calling it the Strait of America.

In the face of gas averaging around $4.20 per gallon nationwide (as of this writing), and with no signs those numbers will drop significantly anytime soon, many of our readers have started budgeting to account for high fuel prices. Meanwhile, others are scouring their cities to find the best possible price. Right now, memberships and rewards programs are hands down the best ways to get a substantial discount at the fuel pump, though some good deals are unfortunately drying up, forcing buyers to pivot to new methods to secure the best price in town.

The most notable loss in recent weeks has been the death of the Kroger gas discount. Fortunately, Costco, Love's, Walmart, and other gas and grocery chains still have worthwhile incentives that can save you a ton at the gas station. If you're filling up a big tank or driving a lot, such deals stand to save you a lot of money for the foreseeable future. Stack these savings with a credit card with good rewards for gas purchases, and you might even be able to convince yourself it's 2024 again and gas prices are hovering just above $3 per gallon.

The first rewards program gas discount on the list is only temporary, but it's a big one. Regular Save Mart shoppers are going to want to strike while the iron is hot because this West Coast grocer is offering up to $1 off per gallon at participating Shell locations, but only through the end of 2026. Signing up to be a Save Mart Rewards member is free, and a dollar spent in store equals one point. You can turn 100 points into 10 cents off per gallon, and this benefit stacks up to 1,000 points for a total of $1 per gallon off. You can use these points at the pump by providing your Save Mart-associated phone number at a participating station.

If you live in Save Mart's service area, you're probably staring down gas prices of around $5.50 per gallon, so this gas deal represents up to 18% off at the pump. Not bad at all, though of course it requires spending about $1,000 on qualifying groceries to unlock the full discount. This deal was initially scheduled to end in September of 2026, and was extended, so there's a chance you'll be able to find it next year, too, but don't count on the supermarket's biggest fuel deal ever lasting that much longer.

There's some fine print you'll want to know about, too. First, you're limited to 20 gallons per fill-up, for a maximum savings of $20. Second, Save Mart points don't last forever. They expire around three months after they're earned, so you're heavily incentivized to use them regularly rather than accumulating points and waiting for the best deals to drop each year.

Perpetual fan-favorite wholesaler Costco promises deals of all types all the time. Those $1.50 hot dogs are famous for a reason, and they really are a helluva deal, but Costco fans swear by their gas prices. Full disclosure: I'm one of those people. Their fuel deals aren't part of a rewards program in the traditional sense. There's no spending to accumulate points and then spending points for further deals. Instead, access to Costco gas stations is locked behind a $65 per year membership that includes online and in-person wholesale shopping, membership for two people, and a long list of benefits from prescriptions and eye exams to car maintenance and insurance offerings. A Costco membership also gets you discounts on Volkswagen SUVs, if you're in the market for a new ride.

The elephant in the room with getting your gas from Costco is the frankly unbelievable lines you might see there. I actually refused to go for a long time, as the lines looked like too much of a headache to be worth the savings. However, Costco pushes fuel to a high volume of drivers surprisingly efficiently, thanks to their numerous pumps and clear signage that indicate when a new pump has opened up and who gets to use it. I've rarely had to wait more than a couple of minutes, and for 10 to 20 cents of savings per gallon, the wait is well worth it.

If you're trying to eke out as much value as possible, you can also sign up for the brand's credit card for 5% back on gas bought at Costco. Those who refill weekly can recover their membership fee with ease.

Love's Travel Stops have a lovable history, as well as a respectable business model, and of all the things they do right, their gas reward program might just be the cherry on top. One aspect of the program that sets it apart from much of the competition is that the Love's Rewards program takes a two-tiered approach, offering different incentives for "casual" drivers and those who take to the road as a profession.

For non-pros, this rewards program offers one point per gallon of fuel purchases, two points per dollar spent in the store, and an automatic 10 cents off every gallon of gasoline. Unlike the Save Mart program, points don't expire as long as your account remains in good standing and stays active. Additionally, members get up to 25 cents off auto diesel purchases. The Love's app also gets you access to basic Wi-Fi at travel stops as well as mobile deals and the ability to order ahead at their connected restaurants.

Professional drivers get assigned a membership tier based on how much fuel they've purchased in any given month. It starts at Base for up to 499 gallons purchased, Gold is unlocked at 500 gallons, and the Platinum and Diamond tiers start at 1,000 and 1,500 gallons, respectively. Members get benefits like free showers and drink refills depending on their tier and earn scaling points for gallons fueled, dollars spent in-store, and dollars spent on truck care. These incentives make OTR trucking just a little bit easier and a little bit more comfortable, which can go a long way to ensuring drivers stay safe and happy on the road.

The Albertsons forU program works like most other grocery store rewards programs, but it has one of the most impressive fuel rewards deals out there. Like other such programs, it unlocks personalized deals, digital coupons, and the occasional free item, and it can also recommend meal plans that include recipes you can add the entirety of to your cart with the click of a button. You get one point per dollar spent on groceries, though these points expire at the end of the month after they're acquired, which is a faster turnaround than even the Save Mart program. If you're the type of person who likes to give gift cards for the holidays, you can earn points faster, though, with a rate of two points per dollar. There are also periodic multiplier events to help you rack up points.

The gas perks apply to gas stations across the country, and the membership generally saves you 10 cents per gallon at Walmart fueling stations, as well as CITGO, Mobil, Murphy, and Exxon stations. For those with Sam's Club memberships, though, the discount doesn't stack. Instead, Walmart+ simply gets you access to Sam's Club stations at Sam's Club member prices. If you find yourself in Alabama, you may also notice the discount isn't consistent, landing somewhere between five and 10 cents depending on the location.

Getting the gas perk requires keeping the Walmart app on your phone, and you'll either need to scan a QR code at the pump or use a discount ID provided by the app. It's not as convenient as other options, but it's still a solid discount. This option doesn't earn your membership money back quite as fast as the Costco offer does, though, so it's probably reserved for people who can take as much advantage of the other perks as possible.

#5777. Consumer Reports' Three Most Reliable Used Sub-$25K 3-Row SUVs

Crossovers and SUVs account for more than 50% of all new car sales, but despite that, finding a reliable three-row model that doesn't break the bank isn't always easy. The cheapest three-row SUV you can buy – the now hybrid-only Mitsubishi Outlander – costs over $32,000 before options. So, if your budget is around $25,000 and you have a big family that needs a big car, going for a used model that has already gone through its steepest part of its depreciation is a solid choice. The good news is that there are plenty of used options at that price, but the big question is whether you'll find one you can rely on and ease the pressure of rising living costs.

Thankfully, the analysts at Consumer Reports (CR) have gathered the best minivans and three-row SUVs and selected the most reliable options you can buy used on a $25,000 budget in one place. Each one of these offers the blend of everyday practicality, comfort, and dependability you'll appreciate, whether you need it for long-distance holiday trips, a school run, or a morning commute. Although both SUVs and minivans were considered, every car in the top three was an SUV, suggesting SUVs came out ahead for reliability at this price point. Let's see how they compare and why they made CR's reliability shortlist.

Consumer Reports rated the 2021 Honda Pilot above average in reliability and third among all SUVs released for that model year. As Honda's biggest SUV, the Pilot is as family-friendly as it gets at this price point. It's packed with a variety of clever storage solutions, strong safety tech, enough room to accommodate kids and tall adults, and up to a cavernous 109 cubic feet of maximum cargo area, so it should easily accommodate bulky items, too. Additionally, you get rear seat backrests that split and fold 60/40, along with advanced safety features like adaptive cruise control, lane-keep assist, automatic high-beam headlights, and forward collision warning with automatic braking.

And if those base features aren't enough, higher trims such as the Pilot EX, EX-L, SE, and Touring are also available within our $25,000 budget, as the 2021 Pilot hasn't resisted depreciation well. Depending on your trim of choice, you can get additional features such as wireless smartphone charging, heated front seats, heated rear seats, a sunroof, and a hands-free liftgate. While sub-100,000-mile examples regularly fetch over $20,000, scroll through CarGurus' listings, and you'll find the cheapest examples cost around $13,000, but these have covered well over 100,000 miles. Whether it's a base version or any of the range-topping models, the Pilot offers one engine option to meet your performance needs: a 3.5-liter naturally aspirated V6 good for 280 horsepower and 262 lb-ft.

In general, Toyota models do well when it comes to reliability. The 2019 Highlander lives up to that reputation, earning well above average in Consumer Reports' survey. Looking through CarGurus listings, the 2019 Highlander is also proving to be exceptionally durable, as we regularly see examples with well over 250,000 miles on the clock looking for a new owner. Such mega-mileage models are priced from around $13,000, but for a little more (around $17,000), you'll find sub-100,000-mile examples that haven't had a hard life.

If you're considering the base-spec LE trim, it comes standard with a 6.1-inch touchscreen, 18-inch alloy wheels, heated mirrors, and a 2.7-liter inline four-cylinder engine making 185 horsepower and 184 lb-ft of torque.  This means if you want gobs of power, you'll find the LE Plus or higher trims to be the keener bargains. Those models are equipped with a 3.5-liter V6 that outputs 295 horsepower and 263 lb-ft. Along with being more powerful, the V6-powered Highlanders are also a tad more efficient than their four-cylinder siblings, returning 27 mpg on the highway and 23 mpg combined versus 24 and 22 mpg for models with the 2.7-liter inline-4, respectively.

If a good miles-per-gallon rating matters very much, you could skip the nonhybrid Highlanders altogether and go with the Toyota Highlander Hybrid instead. It gets up to 29 mpg combined from a hybrid setup comprising a 3.5-liter V6 engine paired with 650-volt AC permanent-magnet synchronous electric motors. The efficiency didn't come at the expense of power either, since owners get up to 306 horsepower to play with. Not to mention, the 2018 Highlander Hybrid's reliability is stellar as well, considering CR ranked the second most reliable model among 2018 SUVs. And for times when you need to move the entire family, there's enough room inside to help you deal with family life, even if space is tighter in the third row. There, occupants make do with 35.9 inches of headroom and 27.7 inches of legroom.

That's a big drop from the 39.9 inches of headroom and 38.4 inches of legroom enjoyed by those in the second row, and it's even less than in front, where there's 40.7 inches of headroom and 44.2 inches of legroom. Space is also at a premium on the cargo side of things, with the Highlander offering 13.8 cubic feet with all seats in use, 42.3 cubic feet behind the second row, and a maximum 83.7 cubic feet behind the first. Around $13,000 will get you into a high-mileage 2018 Toyota Highlander Hybrid in good working order, but models with less than 60,000 miles still cost up to around $35,000.
